title: Parish and Letter
premise: True-crime podcaster Gideon Amberdale has spent years solving small-town deaths the police mislabeled as accidents, all while hiding a secret: their own family fled the parish of Wexcombe thirty years ago under suspicion of murder. When the town's revered founder, Edmund Parish, is exhumed and his coffin proves empty, Gideon realizes the founder's death certificate—the case that drove their family out—was a fiction, and the 'body' may never have existed. As Gideon digs into alibis woven three decades ago, they uncover a living conspiracy among Wexcombe's founding families, one that has already begun killing again to protect the legend. In the end, Gideon must choose between publishing the truth and shielding the one person who showed them love against duty: the dying constable who falsified the original report to save a child—Gideon themselves.
about_author: M. M. Thornbury is the pen name of a former parish archivist who spent fifteen years cataloguing birth, death, and burial registers in the English countryside before turning to fiction. They write mysteries about the lies small communities tell to survive, and they still cannot pass a churchyard without checking the dates on the stones.

chapters.title: The Weight of Empty Earth
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Gideon's POV. Gideon attends the exhumation of founder Edmund Parish, expecting a formality for a heritage plaque. When the coffin is lifted, it is conspicuously light—and inside, only a ledger wrapped in oilcloth. The gravedigger crosses himself. Gideon's instinct for buried lies ignites. Emotional beat: the thrill of a puzzle that is also a door swinging open onto Gideon's own buried past.

chapters.title: Three Accidents, One Signature
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. In their rented room above the Wexcombe archive, Gideon reviews the podcast's three solved cases and notices all three death certificates carry the same counter-signature: Constable R. Halloway—the same officer who signed Edmund Parish's certificate in 1994. Gideon realizes the pattern is not coincidence but a hand. Emotional beat: unease curdling into recognition; the past is not past.

chapters.title: The Founders' Bench
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. At the village fete, Gideon interviews the Parish Trust's chair, Verity Coldbrook, who is charming and precisely unhelpful. Gideon notes who flinches at Edmund's name and who performs grief. A teenage volunteer, Sela, slips Gideon a photocopied page from the 1994 burial register—the entry is in different ink than the rest. Emotional beat: the town as a stage, and Gideon an audience member who knows the script.

chapters.title: What the Archive Keeps
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Deep in the parish archive, Gideon finds the burial ledger Sela copied from, and beside it, a 1994 letter addressed to their mother—unopened, redirected, returned. Their family name, Amberdale, appears on a list of 'persons of interest' in Halloway's hand. Emotional beat: the cold shock of discovering the case they are investigating has been waiting for them all along.

chapters.title: Halloway's Long Silence
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon visits retired Constable Rowan Halloway, now a frail widower tending bees. He is courteous, evasive, and visibly frightened when Edmund's name comes up. He warns Gideon: 'Some graves are empty because the town needed them to be.' Emotional beat: Gideon recognizes in Halloway the same loneliness they carry—two keepers of the same secret, thirty years apart.

chapters.title: Episode One: The Founder
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, interwoven with podcast transcript excerpts. Gideon releases a carefully redacted episode on the empty coffin, using it as bait. Within a day, Verity Coldbrook requests a meeting, and an anonymous email threatens the podcast's hosting. Someone in Wexcombe is listening very closely. Emotional beat: the intoxicating, dangerous power of an audience.

chapters.title: Sela's Inheritance
chapters.summary: Sela's POV, first appearance. Sela, the archivist's granddaughter, reveals she has been reading the restricted ledgers for years because her grandmother's death in 1998 was also called an accident. She wants in. Gideon hesitates—then sees their younger self in her. Emotional beat: the first thread of found family, chosen deliberately.

chapters.title: The Alibi of the Founding Families
chapters.summary: Gideon and Sela's POV alternating. They map the night of Edmund's supposed death: five founding families, five alibis, all corroborating each other in a neat, rehearsed circle. Gideon identifies the seam—two alibis that overlap in a way that means one of the five was never at the dinner at all. Emotional beat: the satisfaction of the craft, shadowed by the knowledge that these are still powerful people.

chapters.title: A Fire in the Filing Room
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. The parish archive burns in the night. Gideon arrives to find Sela unharmed but the 1990s ledgers destroyed—except the page Sela already copied. A fire marshal finds accelerant traces and a melted padlock that was never locked. Emotional beat: fear sharpening into resolve; the enemy has moved from silence to violence.

chapters.title: Verity's Bargain
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Verity Coldbrook offers Gideon access to the Trust's private papers in exchange for editorial control of the podcast's finale. She speaks of Edmund as a father, a saint, a load-bearing wall of the town. Gideon accepts, lying easily, and hates how easily. Emotional beat: love against duty begins its first argument—truth versus the people who need the lie.

chapters.title: The Ledger in Oilcloth
chapters.summary: Sela's POV. Sela deciphers the ledger from the coffin: it is Edmund's own hand, a record of payments made to the five founding families across decades—hush money in reverse. Edmund was blackmailing his own legend into existence. The last entry, dated after his death certificate, reads only: 'They think I am gone. Let them.' Emotional beat: the vertigo of a victim who may be the author of everything.

chapters.title: What Halloway Buried
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Halloway, pressed by the fire and his own conscience, admits he signed false certificates—including the 1994 one—to protect a child who witnessed something in the Parish house that night. He will not say the child's name. Gideon already knows. Emotional beat: the ground giving way; Gideon's whole investigation has been a circle drawn around themselves.

chapters.title: The Amberdale File
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, with flashback fragments. Gideon confronts their own history: the family's midnight departure from Wexcombe, the mother's refusal ever to speak of it, the aunt who raised them. The witness was seven-year-old Gideon, who saw a man alive who was officially dead. Emotional beat: grief and relief tangled together—the coldest case was always their own.

chapters.title: If Edmund Lives
chapters.summary: Sela and Gideon's POV. If Edmund Parish walked out of his own funeral, he is either dead since, hiding, or—impossibly—still alive at ninety-one. They trace pension payments and a private nursing cottage on the Coldbrook land. Someone has been visiting it every Sunday for thirty years. Emotional beat: hope and horror arriving in the same carriage.

chapters.title: The Sunday Visitor
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon watches the cottage and sees Verity Coldbrook arrive with flowers and a covered dish—tending, all these years, the man whose legend is the town's foundation. Confronting her, Gideon learns Verity has known since she was nineteen, and has kept him hidden out of love, not conspiracy. Emotional beat: the theme made flesh—love against duty, wearing Verity's face.

chapters.title: The Fourth Accident
chapters.summary: Sela's POV. Halloway is found drowned in his bee-yard water trough—ruled, preliminarily, a fall. Sela finds his beekeeping gloves folded neatly beside the trough; Halloway never worked without them on. Someone is executing the old pattern one last time, and Sela is the only one who sees it. Emotional beat: fury and terror; the cost of the truth is now being paid in blood.

chapters.title: Who Needed Him Dead
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon re-examines the founding families' descendants: one, Martin Quill, has been quietly buying up Parish Trust debt and stands to control Wexcombe outright if the legend—and its living, inconvenient author—can be managed. Quill's father signed the 1994 alibi circle. The son is finishing the job. Emotional beat: the mystery's gears meshing; justice outside the law becomes not a philosophy but a necessity, because the law keeps signing the wrong certificates.

chapters.title: The Cottage at Night
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Gideon and Sela reach the cottage to move Edmund to safety and find signs of a struggle—blood, a broken teacup, Edmund gone. Verity is bound and gagged inside. She whispers Quill's name. Emotional beat: the trap closing; every move Gideon has made publicly has been read by the enemy all along.

chapters.title: Where the Founder Walks
chapters.summary: Gideon and Sela's POV. Following Edmund's lifelong habit—his nightly walk to the churchyard to look at his own grave—they deduce Quill will force the old man to the one place that legitimizes a death: his own memorial stone, where a fresh burial would explain a fresh body. They race through the fog to the churchyard. Emotional beat: dread and clarity fused; the geography of the whole book converging on six feet of empty earth.

chapters.title: The Grave and the Living Man
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Climax. In the churchyard, Quill forces Edmund to sign a final 'confession' recanting the ledger, intending to bury the old man alive in his own plot—closing the case forever. Gideon intervenes, recording everything live on the podcast feed as Sela leads Verity and the constabulary in. Quill, exposed to the whole listening town, breaks. Emotional beat: the climax as an act of witness—justice achieved not by force but by making the town hear what it spent thirty years refusing to.

chapters.title: The Constable's Testimony
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. In the aftermath, Gideon faces the choice: the full story requires exposing Halloway's falsified certificates—and their own family's flight. Halloway, before dying, left a recorded confession taking full responsibility and naming Gideon's mother as an innocent witness. Gideon edits the final episode to tell everything but to let Halloway's own voice carry the weight. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into mercy; justice that does not require devouring the man who broke rules for love.

chapters.title: Parish and Letter
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV, closing. Edmund Parish, frail and unrepentant about his blackmail but grateful, is quietly relocated; Verity visits him still. Gideon stays in Wexcombe, takes over the archive with Sela, and begins a new episode series—not cold cases, but the town's living story. The final scene: Gideon places flowers on Halloway's grave and on the empty plot beside it, at peace with both. Emotional beat: found family settled into its house; the letter finally answered.
